pos: n. (a secondary wife of lesser legal standing; rendering Hebrew pilegesh)
etymology: From Latin concubina, from con, with, and cubare, to lie down. The Hebrew pilegesh denotes a woman genuinely attached to a household with real if inferior standing — not a mistress, and not a wife.
biblical_def: A concubine in the Old Testament is a secondary wife: a woman legally joined to a man's household, whose children were recognised but who did not hold the standing or inheritance rights of a wife. Scripture records the practice without ever commending it, and every narrative involving one is a disaster. Abraham takes Hagar at Sarai's suggestion and produces a division that outlives them both (Genesis 16:3), then sends the sons of his concubines away with gifts so that Isaac alone inherits (Genesis 25:6). Solomon's establishment is stated in figures that read as an indictment: “he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart” (1 Kings 11:3) — and the sentence ends where Deuteronomy 17:17 said it would. In the house of Saul a concubine becomes the pretext for a political rupture: “Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” (2 Samuel 3:7). And Absalom's public seizure of David's concubines on the palace roof (2 Samuel 16:22) is the exact fulfilment of Nathan's word against David's own adultery. The book of Judges closes with the outrage against a Levite's concubine and a civil war, under the refrain that there was no king in Israel and every man did that which was right in his own eyes. The Bible's method here is narrative rather than statute: it lets the institution destroy every house that adopts it.
webster_summary: A secondary wife of lesser standing. Scripture records the practice without commending it — Hagar divides Abraham's house, Solomon's wives turn away his heart, Absalom seizes David's concubines in fulfilment of Nathan's word, and Judges ends in civil war over one.
webster_full: CONCUBINE, n. [L. concubina; con and cubo, to lie down.] A woman who cohabits with a man, without the authority of a legal marriage.
2. A wife of inferior condition; a lawful wife, but not united to the man by the usual ceremonies, and of inferior condition. Such were Hagar and Keturah, the concubines of Abraham.
3. Among the Hebrews, the concubine's children were not heirs with the children of the wife, but received gifts.
4. In modern usage, a kept mistress.
5. The distinction of wife and concubine was recognized in the civil law.
scriptures: 1 Kings 11:3
And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart.
Genesis 25:6
But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country.
2 Samuel 3:7
And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?
2 Samuel 16:22
So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
corruption_summary: That the Bible records concubinage is treated as evidence that the Bible approves it — used by sceptics to indict Scripture's sexual ethic and by others to relativise the one-man-one-woman standard.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument is familiar: the patriarchs had concubines, therefore biblical marriage was never monogamous, therefore the modern church's standard is a later imposition. The confusion is between description and prescription, and Scripture guards against it in the clearest possible way — by outcome. Every household in the Bible that takes a concubine is wrecked by it. Abraham's produces Ishmael and a conflict still running; Jacob's produces a family so fractured that the brothers sell one of their own; David's produces Amnon, Tamar, and Absalom; Solomon's produces apostasy and a divided kingdom; the Levite's produces a massacre. Meanwhile the creation ordinance stands untouched from Genesis 2:24, and the Lord Jesus goes behind every subsequent accommodation to it: from the beginning it was not so (Matthew 19:8). The narrative is not endorsement; it is a long argument by consequence.

There is a further point that the sceptical reading misses entirely, and it is to Scripture's credit rather than its embarrassment. The Bible tells these stories against its own heroes. Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon are the founding figures of the nation, and the text records their concubinage and its ruin in full, with no attempt to tidy the record. Rizpah, a concubine used as a political counter by men on both sides, is given one of the most dignified scenes in the histories, keeping the birds off her sons' bodies until the rains came (2 Samuel 21:10). A propaganda literature does not write that scene. The women in these narratives are treated by the men as instruments and by the text as persons, and the gap between those two treatments is the judgment.
roots_summary: Hebrew pilegesh (a concubine, secondary wife), a word of uncertain and probably non-Semitic origin; Greek pallake in the Septuagint; the New Testament has no equivalent because the practice has no place in it.
roots_lines: Hebrew pilegesh (H6370) — concubine, secondary wife; used of Hagar, Bilhah, Zilpah, Rizpah, and the Levite's woman in Judges 19.
Hebrew ishshah (H802) — woman, wife; the standard term, and notably applied to Hagar in Genesis 16:3, showing the standing was real if inferior.
Hebrew amah (H519) and shiphchah (H8198) — maidservant, handmaid; the status from which several concubines were taken.
Greek pallake — the Septuagint rendering; the term does not occur in the Greek New Testament.
Hebrew debaq (H1692) — to cleave; the verb of Genesis 2:24 that defines the one union concubinage sets aside.
usage: “His wives turned away his heart” — the verdict on the largest household of concubines in Scripture.
“Sent them away from Isaac his son” — the inheritance line runs through the wife, not the concubine.
“In the sight of all Israel” — Absalom's public act, and the exact terms of Nathan's word to David.

pos: n. (a woman who has not known a man; rendering Hebrew almah, bethulah, Greek parthenos)
etymology: From Latin virgo. The contested Hebrew term is almah, a young woman of marriageable age, which in every one of its Old Testament occurrences denotes an unmarried woman and which the pre-Christian Jewish translators of the Septuagint rendered by the unambiguous Greek parthenos.
biblical_def: A virgin is a woman who has not known a man, and the word carries the weight of the incarnation. Isaiah gives the sign to the house of David: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:14), and Matthew cites it as fulfilled in Mary, “a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary” (Luke 1:27). The doctrine is not ornamental. If Christ were begotten in the ordinary way He would be a son of Adam by natural generation and would stand under the imputation of Adam's sin like every other man; the virgin conception is how the second Adam enters the race without inheriting its guilt, while taking a true human nature from a true human mother. The word then becomes a figure for the church's exclusive fidelity: “I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2), where Paul's jealousy is stirred by false apostles rather than by pagan neighbours — the threat to virginity is doctrinal. And the Lord Jesus makes ten virgins His parable of readiness: “Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom” (Matthew 25:1) — where all ten are virgins, all ten have lamps, all ten sleep, and five are shut out for want of oil.
webster_summary: A woman who has not known a man. Isaiah's sign and Luke's narrative give the church the virgin conception, by which the second Adam enters the race without its guilt; Paul makes the church a chaste virgin espoused to one husband.
webster_full: VIRGIN, n. [L. virgo.] A woman who has had no carnal knowledge of man; a maid.
2. A woman not a mother; as, the virgin queen.
3. Any thing untouched or unmixed; as virgin gold.
VIRGIN, a. Pure; untouched; as virgin snow.
4. In Scripture, applied figuratively to a city or people, as the virgin daughter of Zion; and to the church, espoused as a chaste virgin to Christ. 2 Cor. 11.
scriptures: Isaiah 7:14
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Luke 1:27
To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary.
2 Corinthians 11:2
For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
Matthew 25:1
Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 7:14 is re-translated as young woman to sever the prophecy from the virgin birth, and the doctrine itself is recast as a devotional legend the modern believer may hold loosely — while Rome inflates it in the opposite direction into perpetual virginity and immaculate conception.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical case runs that almah means only a young woman, that Hebrew has a precise word for virgin in bethulah, and that Matthew read the Septuagint carelessly. Three things answer it. First, bethulah is not unambiguous either — Joel 1:8 has a bethulah lamenting the husband of her youth. Second, every occurrence of almah in the Old Testament denotes an unmarried young woman, and there is no instance where the word describes a woman known to have had relations. Third and most decisively, the Septuagint translators rendered it parthenos, the unambiguous Greek term, roughly two centuries before Christ and with no Christian motive whatever. Matthew did not invent the reading; he inherited it from Jewish scholarship. And the sign given to Ahaz is announced as something the Lord Himself would give — a young woman bearing a child in the ordinary way is not a sign at all.

The doctrinal stakes explain why this verse is fought over. Deny the virgin conception and either Christ is an ordinary man later adopted, which is the ancient adoptionist heresy, or He is God in a body that is not truly human, which is docetism; and in either case He is disqualified as the last Adam who is both true man and free of Adam's guilt. Rome errs in the opposite direction, extending Mary's virginity perpetually and adding an immaculate conception of her own, both of which the Scriptures nowhere teach and the second of which implies that sinlessness required a second miracle — an argument that, followed consistently, regresses forever. Matthew records that Joseph knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son (Matthew 1:25), and the Gospels name the Lord's brothers plainly. The dictionary honours Mary as the blessed and believing mother of the Lord and declines the additions.
roots_summary: Hebrew almah (a young woman of marriageable age, unmarried) and bethulah (a virgin, maiden); Greek parthenos (a virgin), the Septuagint's rendering of almah in Isaiah 7:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew almah (H5959) — a young woman of marriageable age; the word in Isaiah 7:14, used seven times and never of a married woman.
Hebrew bethulah (H1330) — a maiden, virgin; the more common term, though not itself free of ambiguity (Joel 1:8).
Greek parthenos (G3933) — a virgin; the Septuagint rendering of Isaiah 7:14 and the word in Matthew 1:23, Luke 1:27, and 2 Corinthians 11:2.
Hebrew Immanuel (H6005) — God with us; the name given to the child of the sign.
Greek hagnos (G53) — pure, chaste; the adjective Paul joins to parthenos in 2 Corinthians 11:2.
usage: “The Lord himself shall give you a sign” — a sign God gives is not an ordinary birth.
“A chaste virgin to Christ” — the church's fidelity, threatened by false apostles rather than by pagans.
“Ten virgins, which took their lamps” — all ten virgins, all ten with lamps, and five shut out.

pos: adj. (unable to bear children; unfruitful; rendering Hebrew aqar, Greek steira, argos)
etymology: From Old French baraigne, sterile. In Scripture the word governs one of the Bible's most persistent patterns: the promised line repeatedly runs through a womb that cannot produce it.
biblical_def: Barren means unable to bear, and Scripture returns to the condition so often that it becomes a doctrine. The first thing said of the mother of the covenant people is a negative: “But Sarai was barren; she had no child” (Genesis 11:30) — stated immediately before God promises Abram a nation. Rebekah is barren, Rachel is barren, Manoah's wife is barren, Hannah is barren, and Elisabeth is barren: “they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years” (Luke 1:7). The pattern is not incidental. Every decisive figure in redemptive history — Isaac, Jacob, Samson, Samuel, John the Baptist — is born to a woman who could not have him, so that the line of promise visibly does not run on human capacity, and the sequence ends with a virgin, where human capacity is not merely weak but absent. The Psalter turns the reversal into praise: “He maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children” (Psalm 113:9). Isaiah gives the barren woman a song before there is anything to sing about: “Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear… for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife” (Isaiah 54:1), which Paul applies to the covenant of promise. Peter then transfers the word to the moral life: the man in whom the Christian graces abound “shall neither be barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 1:8).
webster_summary: Unable to bear. Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and Elisabeth are all barren, so that the promised line visibly does not run on human capacity; Psalm 113 and Isaiah 54 make the reversal a song, and Peter applies the word to fruitless profession.
webster_full: BARREN, a. Not producing young, or offspring; applied to animals.
2. Not producing plants; unfruitful; sterile; not fertile; as barren land.
3. Not producing the usual fruit; as a barren tree.
4. Unmeaning; uninstructive; as a barren discourse.
5. Not copious; scanty; as a barren subject. Neither barren nor unfruitful. 2 Pet. 1.
scriptures: Genesis 11:30
But Sarai was barren; she had no child.
Luke 1:7
And they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years.
Psalm 113:9
He maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children. Praise ye the LORD.
Isaiah 54:1

Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Barrenness is preached as evidence of divine displeasure or of insufficient faith — a cruelty the Bible's own narratives contradict, since the women it names as barren are among the most honoured in Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the prosperity teaching is at work, a childless couple is told that a promise unclaimed, a sin unconfessed, or a faith too small stands between them and the child. Scripture's roster of barren women is the standing refutation: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and Elisabeth, of whom Luke says expressly that she and Zacharias were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless — and they had no child (Luke 1:6-7). The two facts sit in consecutive verses precisely so that no one can join them causally. Hannah's account adds that it was the LORD who had shut up her womb (1 Samuel 1:5), which is harder and more comforting than the alternative: her sorrow was under God's hand, not outside it, and He was doing something with it she could not yet see. Peninnah's provocation is recorded as cruelty, and every counsellor who repeats it is standing in Peninnah's place.

The other corruption is a modern reading of Psalm 113:9 and Isaiah 54:1 that hears them as sentimental consolation. They are stronger than that. Psalm 113 sets the barren woman's joy in the same stanza as God raising the poor out of the dust and setting him with princes; it is a psalm about the reversal of settled conditions by a God who dwells on high and humbles Himself to behold. Isaiah 54:1 commands singing before the children arrive, and Paul cites it in Galatians 4:27 of the Jerusalem above — the barren woman's children are the whole church of the promise. Scripture neither minimises the grief nor leaves it where it found it, and it never once attributes it to the sufferer's failure.
roots_summary: Hebrew aqar (barren, from a root meaning to pluck up by the roots); Greek steira (barren, sterile) and argos (idle, unproductive — the word in 2 Peter 1:8).
roots_lines: Hebrew aqar (H6135) — barren, sterile; used of Sarai, Rebekah, Rachel, Manoah's wife, and Hannah.
Hebrew aqar (H6131) — to pluck up by the roots; the cognate verb, giving the noun its force of something uprooted.
Greek steira (G4723) — barren, sterile; the word for Elisabeth in Luke 1:7 and in the citation of Isaiah 54:1 at Galatians 4:27.
Greek argos (G692) — idle, unemployed, unproductive; the word rendered barren in 2 Peter 1:8.
Greek akarpos (G175) — without fruit, unfruitful; the companion term in 2 Peter 1:8 and in the parable of the sower.
usage: “But Sarai was barren” — stated immediately before the promise of a nation.
“They were both righteous before God… and they had no child” — two facts Luke places side by side so no one can join them.
“Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear” — the song commanded before the children arrive.

pos: v.t. and v.i. (to enter the covenant union of husband and wife; rendering Hebrew laqach, ba'al, Greek gameo)
etymology: From Old French marier, Latin maritare, from maritus, a husband. Scripture's own vocabulary is plainer — Hebrew commonly says a man takes a wife, and the taking is a public, covenantal act with witnesses.
biblical_def: To marry is to enter the covenant union established at creation, which the Lord Jesus grounds not in Moses but in Genesis: God made them male and female, and “For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh” (Ephesians 5:31, citing Genesis 2:24). Three acts constitute it — leaving, cleaving, and becoming one flesh — in that order, so that a public separation from the parental household precedes the union rather than following it. Paul treats marriage as the ordinary and honourable estate while granting that singleness has real advantages for undivided service, and he is entirely unsentimental about the reason many should marry: “if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9). He instructs the younger widows likewise: “I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully” (1 Timothy 5:14). Hebrews states the estate's honour and its boundary in one verse: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge” (Hebrews 13:4). And the Lord Jesus sets its horizon: “in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22:30). Marriage is a creation ordinance for this age, pointing beyond itself to the union it pictures.
webster_summary: To enter the creation covenant of one man and one woman. Christ grounds it in Genesis; Paul commends it plainly, including as a remedy for incontinence; Hebrews calls it honourable in all; and Christ says it does not continue in the resurrection.
webster_full: MARRY, v.t. [Fr. marier; L. maritus, a husband.] To unite in wedlock or matrimony; to join a man and woman for life, and constitute them man and wife according to the laws or customs of a nation.
2. To dispose of in wedlock; as, a father marries his daughter.
3. To take for husband or wife.
MARRY, v.i. To enter into the conjugal state; to unite as husband and wife.
5. It is better to marry than to burn. 1 Cor. 7.
scriptures: Ephesians 5:31
For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.
1 Corinthians 7:9
But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
Hebrews 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Matthew 22:30
For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.
corruption_summary: Marriage has been redefined from a covenant instituted by God between one man and one woman into a contract of mutual satisfaction terminable at will, and then extended to unions Scripture does not recognise — while a rival error inside the church denigrates it as second-best to celibacy.
corruption_paragraphs: Two redefinitions have proceeded together, and the first made the second possible. Once marriage was recast as a private arrangement for the happiness of the parties, its permanence became negotiable, its exclusivity optional, and the sexes of the parties incidental — because a contract of mutual satisfaction has no principle limiting it. Scripture's account is different at the root: marriage is a creation ordinance, established before the fall, instituted by God rather than by the couple or the state, with a Witness present at every wedding, and it is the appointed picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32). That is why the sexes are not incidental — the picture requires a husband and a bride — and why permanence is not a preference. The dictionary holds the one-man-one-woman-for-life standard as the Lord Jesus stated it in Matthew 19, with the single exception He named, and holds it with pastoral care for the many whose marriages have failed, since a standard restated is not a stone thrown.

The opposite corruption is older and arose inside the church: the elevation of celibacy into a higher spiritual state, with marriage tolerated as a concession to weakness. It produced enforced clerical celibacy, monastic vows, and the reading of 1 Corinthians 7 as though Paul preferred virginity in principle. Paul says something narrower — that in a present distress the unmarried are freer for undivided service — and he says elsewhere that forbidding to marry is a doctrine of devils (1 Timothy 4:1-3). Hebrews 13:4 settles it: marriage is honourable in all. The Reformers married deliberately and publicly for this reason, and the pastor's household became one of Protestantism's most visible arguments.
roots_summary: Hebrew laqach (to take, as a man takes a wife) and ba'al (to be master of, to marry); Greek gameo (to marry) and gamizo (to give in marriage), with gamos, the wedding itself.
roots_lines: Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take, receive; the ordinary idiom for taking a wife throughout the Old Testament.
Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cleave, cling; the verb of Genesis 2:24 rendered joined unto in Ephesians 5:31.
Greek gameo (G1060) — to marry; the verb in 1 Corinthians 7:9 and Matthew 22:30.
Greek gamos (G1062) — a wedding, marriage feast; the word in Hebrews 13:4 and in the parables of the marriage supper.
Greek mysterion (G3466) — a mystery, a truth once hidden now revealed; Paul's term for what marriage pictures in Ephesians 5:32.
usage: “Leave… be joined… one flesh” — three acts in a fixed order; the public leaving precedes the union.
“Better to marry than to burn” — Paul's entirely unsentimental counsel.
“In the resurrection they neither marry” — a creation ordinance for this age, pointing past itself.

pos: n. (a father or mother; rendering Greek goneus)
etymology: From Latin parens, from parere, to bring forth. The Greek goneus is built the same way, from ginomai — the parent is the one from whom the child came, and Scripture makes that fact the ground of an obligation.
biblical_def: A parent in Scripture holds an office, not merely a relationship, and the fifth commandment attaches to it the first promise: honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long. Paul restates it as the basic ordering of a Christian household: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right” (Ephesians 6:1) — and the ground he gives is not utility but rightness, the creational fitness of the thing. The duty runs both ways and Paul states the parental side memorably: “the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children” (2 Corinthians 12:14), which he uses to explain why he took no money from the Corinthians. Provision flows downward, honour flows upward, and a household that reverses either is disordered. The Lord Jesus qualifies the obedience without abolishing it — the disciple who loves father or mother more than Him is not worthy of Him, and He warns that the gospel will divide households, with children delivered up by parents (Luke 21:16). And Paul makes disobedience to parents a diagnostic of civilisational decay, listing it among the marks of the last days: “men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2 Timothy 3:2) — sandwiched between blasphemy and ingratitude, which is where Scripture thinks it belongs.
webster_summary: A father or mother, holding an office. Children are to obey because it is right; parents lay up for children rather than the reverse; and disobedience to parents is listed among the marks of the last days.
webster_full: PARENT, n. [L. parens, from pario, to bear.] A father or mother; he or she that produces young.
2. That which produces; cause; source; as idleness is the parent of vice.
PARENTAL, a. Pertaining to parents; as parental authority.
3. Becoming parents; tender; affectionate; as parental care.
4. Disobedient to parents, a mark of the perilous times. 2 Tim. 3.
scriptures: Ephesians 6:1
Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right.
2 Corinthians 12:14

Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children.
2 Timothy 3:2
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
Luke 21:16
And ye shall be betrayed both by parents, and brethren, and kinsfolks, and friends; and some of you shall they cause to be put to death.
corruption_summary: Parental authority has been steadily transferred to the state and to the expert class, on the premise that children belong first to society; and inside the church the same commandment is sometimes pressed into a demand for adult obedience it never made.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture assigns the raising of children to parents and to no one else: fathers are to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4), and the commands of Deuteronomy 6 place the teaching of God's word in the house, on the road, at bedtime and at rising. Family, church, and state are three God-ordained authorities with distinct spheres, and the modern drift — in which schooling, medical decisions, and the moral formation of children pass by default to institutions that hold a different account of the good — is a sphere violation whatever its intentions. The dictionary holds the classical position: the state bears a genuine and God-given sword, including against parents who abuse their charge, and it has no commission to replace the household as the child's formative authority.

The opposite abuse belongs to the church and appears wherever the fifth commandment is preached as unlimited. The commandment says honour, and honour is owed lifelong; Paul's word to children is obey, and it is addressed to children under the roof and qualified in the Lord. An adult son owes his father honour, care in age (which the Lord Jesus enforced against the corban evasion in Mark 7:11-13), and a hearing; he does not owe him obedience in the disposal of his own household, and no parent may command what God forbids. Where a movement teaches otherwise — adult children under paternal authority indefinitely, marriages arranged and vetoed — it has taken a real commandment past the point Scripture set for it, and the households it has damaged are the evidence.
roots_summary: Greek goneus (a parent, from ginomai, to come into being); Hebrew uses ab (father) and em (mother) rather than a collective term, which is itself significant — the commandment names them separately.
roots_lines: Greek goneus (G1118) — a parent; the word in Ephesians 6:1, 2 Corinthians 12:14, 2 Timothy 3:2, and Luke 21:16.
Hebrew ab (H1) — father; the first term of the fifth commandment and the root of abba.
Hebrew em (H517) — mother; named alongside the father in the commandment, with equal claim to honour.
Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to be heavy, to honour; the verb of the fifth commandment, whose root sense is to give weight to.
Greek hypakouo (G5219) — to listen under, obey; the verb in Ephesians 6:1, distinct from the honour owed lifelong.
usage: “Obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right” — the ground is creational fitness, and the qualifier is real.
“The parents for the children” — provision runs downward; Paul uses it to explain refusing Corinthian money.
“Disobedient to parents” — listed between blasphemy and ingratitude as a mark of the last days.

pos: n. and adj. (of the sex that bears young; rendering Hebrew neqebah, Greek thelys)
etymology: From Old French femelle, Latin femella, diminutive of femina. The English spelling was later assimilated to male, which the two words do not share etymologically — though Scripture pairs them from the first chapter as a single created distinction.
biblical_def: Female is one half of a created binary established in the first chapter of Scripture, and stated in the same breath as the image of God: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them” (Genesis 1:27). Three claims are packed into that verse. Humanity is one — man, the species. Humanity bears the divine image, both sexes fully and equally. And humanity exists as two sexes by creation, before the fall, so that the distinction is not a result of sin nor a social arrangement but part of what God pronounced very good. The Lord Jesus treats the verse as the settled ground of every question about marriage and sex: “Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4) — the appeal is to the beginning and to what was made. Paul's great equality text does not erase the categories but locates their irrelevance precisely: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). The subject there is standing before God in justification and inheritance, which is identical for all; Paul, who wrote that verse, also wrote the household codes, and did not imagine himself inconsistent.
webster_summary: One half of a creational binary established before the fall and stated alongside the image of God. Christ appeals to male and female from the beginning as settling questions of marriage; Galatians 3:28 makes the sexes equal in standing before God without erasing them.
webster_full: FEMALE, n. [Fr. femelle; L. femella, femina.] Among animals, one of that sex which conceives and brings forth young.
2. Among plants, that which produces fruit; the pistillate plant.
FEMALE, a. Belonging to the sex which produces young; as a female bird.
3. Pertaining to females; as a female school.
4. Male and female created he them. Gen. 1.
scriptures: Genesis 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Matthew 19:4
And he answered and said unto them, Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
Galatians 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Genesis 5:2
Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created.
corruption_summary: The creational category has been detached from the body and relocated in self-perception, so that sex becomes an assignment rather than a fact — and Galatians 3:28 is enlisted to abolish the distinction Paul was assuming.
corruption_paragraphs: The central claim of the present redefinition is that the body reports something provisional and the inner sense reports something authoritative — hence the vocabulary of gender identity, of sex assigned at birth, and of a self whose truth the body may misstate. Genesis 1:27 forecloses it. Sex is created, embodied, and pronounced good before the fall; it is not a costume the self wears nor a label an obstetrician applies. The Lord Jesus, asked about marriage, answered with this verse and with the word made. Scripture's account of the body is high, not low: it is created good, redeemed at cost, indwelt by the Spirit, and destined for resurrection, which is why 1 Corinthians 6 argues morality from the body's ownership rather than from feeling. The dictionary states this without cruelty. Every person is an image-bearer of infinite worth; distress about one's body is real suffering and is met with patience; and no amount of compassion makes a false account of the body true, since a lie has never yet healed anyone.

Galatians 3:28 is the verse most often enlisted against the creational distinction, and its own context defines its scope. Paul's argument from 3:23 onward is about who are the sons of God and heirs according to promise — justification, adoption, inheritance — where Jew and Greek, bond and free, male and female stand on precisely equal ground because all are in Christ by faith and not by descent, status, or sex. He is not abolishing the categories: he does not mean that Jewish identity vanished, or that a slave was thereby freed by his baptism, or that men and women cease to be. The same apostle writes Ephesians 5 and 1 Timothy 2. Equality of standing before God and distinction of office and calling within the church and household are held together throughout the New Testament, and a reading that requires Paul to contradict himself within a few years and a few pages has not understood him.
roots_summary: Hebrew neqebah (female, from a root meaning to pierce or perforate) paired with zakar (male); Greek thelys (female) paired with arsen (male), the pair used in Genesis 1:27 LXX, Matthew 19:4, and Galatians 3:28.
roots_lines: Hebrew neqebah (H5347) — female; the term in Genesis 1:27 and throughout the sacrificial and census legislation.
Hebrew zakar (H2145) — male; the paired term, distinct from the homonymous root meaning to remember.
Greek thelys (G2338) — female; used in Matthew 19:4, Mark 10:6, Romans 1:26-27, and Galatians 3:28.
Greek arsen (G730) — male; the paired term, and the word in Romans 1:27.
Hebrew tselem (H6754) — image; the noun in Genesis 1:27, predicated of the human creature in both sexes.
usage: “Male and female created he them” — the distinction is creational, pre-fall, and stated with the image of God.
“He which made them at the beginning” — Christ's appeal in every question about marriage and sex.
“Neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” — equal standing in justification, not the abolition of the sexes.

pos: n. (an individual human being; in theology, a subsistence in the divine essence; rendering Hebrew panim in idiom, Greek prosopon, hypostasis)
etymology: From Latin persona, originally an actor's mask, then a role, then a legal party. Christian theology took the word and made it carry more than it had ever carried: not a mask over a nature but a genuine subsistence in one.
biblical_def: Person does two jobs in Scripture. In the ethical texts it appears in the idiom of respect of persons — the Hebrew is literally lifting up the face — and it names the sin of judging by the standing rather than the case: “thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour” (Leviticus 19:15). The prohibition cuts both ways, against flattering the powerful and against sentimental favour to the weak, because the standard is the case itself. Moses grounds it in God's own character — He “regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward” (Deuteronomy 10:17) — and Peter, standing in a Gentile house, draws the conclusion the church needed: “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). James makes it a sin without qualification: “if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin” (James 2:9), in a chapter about seating a rich man well and a poor man badly. The word's second job is theological, and Hebrews supplies the term: the Son is “the express image of his person” (Hebrews 1:3), Greek hypostasis — the word the church would use to confess one essence in three Persons, and two natures in one Person.
webster_summary: An individual human being — and in Scripture's idiom, the standing that judges must ignore. God is no respecter of persons and neither may His people be. In theology the word carries the Trinity: one essence, three Persons.
webster_full: PERSON, n. per'sn. [L. persona; said to be from sono, to sound.] An individual human being; a man, woman or child.
2. A man, woman or child, considered as opposed to things, or distinct from them.
3. In theology, one of the three subsistences in the Godhead; as the three persons in the Trinity.
4. In law, an artificial person is a corporation or body politic.
5. Respect of persons, partiality; the favoring of one to the prejudice of another. God is no respecter of persons. Acts 10.
scriptures: Acts 10:34
Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:
Leviticus 19:15
Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.
James 2:9
But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.
Deuteronomy 10:17
For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward:
corruption_summary: “God is no respecter of persons” is quoted to mean that God treats all men identically in salvation — a universalism the phrase does not contain — while Leviticus 19:15's warning against favouring the poor is quietly dropped from the modern conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase means that God does not judge by external standing — nation, rank, wealth, or appearance. It does not mean that God treats all men identically, which would contradict the whole of Scripture: He chose Abraham and not his neighbours, Israel and not Egypt, Jacob and not Esau, and Paul devotes Romans 9 to the objection this raises and answers it with the potter and the clay rather than by denying the premise. Peter's own use fixes the sense — in every nation he that feareth God and worketh righteousness is accepted (Acts 10:35), which is a statement about the abolition of ethnic barriers, spoken as the gospel goes to Cornelius. Election is not respect of persons in the biblical sense precisely because it is not grounded in anything in the person; it is unconditional, which is the opposite of favouritism by rank.

Leviticus 19:15 contains a clause the modern conscience finds counter-intuitive: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor. Scripture's concern for the poor is relentless — the same chapter commands leaving gleanings and forbids oppressing a hired servant — and precisely for that reason it forbids bending a judgment in the poor man's favour. Justice that can be tilted by sympathy can be tilted by anything, and the poor are the first to suffer when courts decide by category rather than by case. Any framework that assigns credibility or guilt by group membership — whichever group is currently favoured — is respect of persons under a new name, and James calls it sin without qualification.
roots_summary: Hebrew idiom nasa panim (to lift up the face, hence to show partiality); Greek prosopolempsia (respect of persons, a New Testament coinage from the same idiom) and hypostasis (substance, subsistence, person).
roots_lines: Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, presence; in the idiom nasa panim, to lift the face, that is, to show partiality.
Greek prosopon (G4383) — face, countenance, person; the literal rendering of the Hebrew idiom.
Greek prosopolemptes (G4381) — a respecter of persons; the coinage in Acts 10:34, formed on the Hebrew idiom.
Greek hypostasis (G5287) — substance, subsistence; the word in Hebrews 1:3 rendered person, and the technical Trinitarian term.
Greek ousia — essence, being; the companion term of the Nicene settlement, one ousia in three hypostaseis.
usage: “God is no respecter of persons” — no judgment by rank or nation; not a statement that God treats all men identically.
“Thou shalt not respect the person of the poor” — the clause the modern conscience skips.
“The express image of his person” — hypostasis, the word the church took up for the Trinity.

pos: n. (one who guards, tends, or has charge of; rendering Hebrew shamar participle, Greek phylax, oikouros)
etymology: English agent-noun from keep. The Hebrew verb behind it, shamar, is the word used of Adam in the garden (to dress it and to keep it) and of God keeping Israel — the same duty, at two scales.
biblical_def: A keeper is one charged with guarding what is not finally his own, and Scripture's first use of the word is a question thrown at God in bad faith: “And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?” (Genesis 4:9). Cain's sneer has become a proverb, generally quoted as though the answer were obvious; the text leaves it unanswered because the whole subsequent Bible is the answer. The word had already been used two verses earlier of Abel's occupation — “Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground” (Genesis 4:2) — so Cain is throwing his murdered brother's own job title back at God. Against that stands the Psalter's most concentrated use of the root, where the same verb appears six times in eight verses: “he that keepeth thee will not slumber” and “The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand” (Psalm 121:3, 5). The pilgrim going up to Jerusalem is told that his safety is not vigilance but a Keeper who does not sleep — a pointed contrast with Baal, of whom Elijah suggested he might be sleeping and need awakening. The office runs down through Scripture: keepers of the door, of the wardrobe, of the prison, of the vineyard, and keepers at home.
webster_summary: One charged with guarding what is not his own. Cain's sneer — Am I my brother's keeper? — is left unanswered because the rest of Scripture answers it; Psalm 121 says the LORD is thy keeper and does not slumber.
webster_full: KEEPER, n. One who keeps; one that holds or has possession of any thing.
2. One who retains in custody; one who has the care of a prison and the custody of prisoners.
3. One who has the care, custody or superintendence of any thing; as the keeper of the great seal; a gamekeeper.
4. One who has the care of flocks or herds; a shepherd. Abel was a keeper of sheep. Gen. 4.
5. A protector; a guardian; as, the Lord is thy keeper. Ps. 121.
scriptures: Genesis 4:9
And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?
Psalm 121:5
The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand.
Psalm 121:3
He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber.
Genesis 4:2
And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.
corruption_summary: Cain's question is quoted approvingly as a defence of privacy and non-interference — and inside the church, as a reason not to pursue an erring brother, which is the one use Scripture most directly forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: “Am I my brother's keeper?” is one of the few Bible verses everyone can quote and one of the few whose speaker is a murderer covering his tracks. It is used now to close conversations: what my neighbour does is his own affair, what I do is mine, and the man who interferes is presumptuous. Scripture's answer, given at length rather than in a sentence, is yes. Every man is his brother's keeper — Leviticus 19:17 requires rebuking a neighbour rather than hating him in the heart, Galatians 6:1 charges the spiritual with restoring the overtaken, and James ends by promising that turning a sinner from the error of his way saves a soul from death. The church's practice of discipline is nothing more than the corporate form of that duty, and its collapse in most congregations is Cain's question adopted as policy.

There is a real counterfeit that has given the objection its force, and it should be named. Keeping a brother is not surveillance, and Scripture puts hard limits on it: Paul forbids suffering as a busybody in other men's matters (1 Peter 4:15), commands that a man study to be quiet and do his own business (1 Thessalonians 4:11), and lays down a procedure in Matthew 18 that begins privately, between two, before anything becomes public. Churches that have inverted this — making every fault a congregational matter, or a leader's knowledge of every household's affairs a mark of care — have not been more faithful than Cain, only differently unfaithful. The keeper of a flock protects it; he does not audit it.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamar (to keep, guard, watch over) — used of Adam keeping the garden, Abel keeping sheep, and the LORD keeping Israel; Greek phylax (a guard) and oikouros (a keeper at home).
roots_lines: Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, observe; the verb repeated six times in Psalm 121 and used of Adam in Genesis 2:15.
Hebrew ro'eh / ro'eh tson — a keeper of sheep, shepherd; Abel's occupation in Genesis 4:2.
Greek phylasso (G5442) — to guard, keep watch; used of keeping the commandments and of God keeping the believer.
Greek phylax (G5441) — a guard, keeper; used of the prison keepers in Acts 5:23 and 12:6.
Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, watch over, preserve; the verb in John 17:11-12, where Christ keeps those given Him.
usage: “Am I my brother's keeper?” — a murderer's evasion, now quoted as a principle.
“The LORD is thy keeper” — the pilgrim's safety is a Keeper, not his own vigilance.
“He that keepeth thee will not slumber” — a pointed contrast with the gods who need waking.

pos: n. (the part of the leg between hip and knee; rendering Hebrew yarek, Greek meros)
etymology: Old English theoh. The Hebrew yarek means the thigh or loins, and by extension the seat of procreative strength — which is why an oath sworn under the thigh is an oath sworn on a man's posterity.
biblical_def: The thigh carries more weight in Scripture than its ordinary anatomy suggests, because Hebrew yarek denotes the seat of generative strength. Hence the strange oath Abraham requires: “Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh” (Genesis 24:2), swearing the servant by the very source of the promised seed — the oath is taken on the covenant line itself, which is why Jacob repeats the gesture with Joseph. The thigh is also where Jacob is permanently marked: “when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him” (Genesis 32:25). The man who had prevailed by grasping since birth is disabled precisely in his strength, and walks away with a new name and a limp; the blessing and the injury arrive in the same moment. Ehud straps his dagger on his right thigh so that a left-handed man passes the guards (Judges 3:16), and the histories are full of such quiet observation. And the thigh appears at the very end of the canon as the place of a title: “he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS” (Revelation 19:16) — written where a rider's sword would hang and where every man on foot would read it.
webster_summary: The seat of generative strength in Hebrew idiom. Oaths are sworn under the thigh, on the covenant line; Jacob is crippled in his at Peniel and leaves with a new name and a limp; and the returning King bears His title on His.
webster_full: THIGH, n. thi. [Sax. theoh.] That part of the leg which is between the knee and the trunk of the body.
2. In Scripture, the loins, as the seat of generative power; whence the phrase, souls that came out of his thigh.
3. To smite hip and thigh, to make a great slaughter. Judges 15.
4. The custom of placing the hand under the thigh in swearing was an ancient and solemn form of oath. Gen. 24.
5. The thigh bone, the femur, the largest bone in the body.
scriptures: Genesis 24:2
And Abraham said unto his eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all that he had, Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh:
Genesis 32:25
And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him.
Revelation 19:16
And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.
Judges 3:16
But Ehud made him a dagger which had two edges, of a cubit length; and he did gird it under his raiment upon his right thigh.
corruption_summary: Jacob's wrestling is preached as a lesson in spiritual persistence — hold on until you get your blessing — while the detail that God crippled him is treated as incidental rather than as the point.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular sermon on Peniel makes Jacob the hero of his own tenacity: he would not let go, he prevailed, and the application is that persistent prayer wins. The narrative resists that at every turn. The wrestler is the one who initiates, who could have ended it at any moment, and who ends it by touching Jacob's thigh out of joint with what reads as almost no effort. Jacob prevails by clinging to a man who has just disabled him and by asking for a blessing he has no claim to — and he is required first to say his own name, which is the name of a supplanter and amounts to a confession. He leaves with a new name, a blessing, and a limp he carries for life. That is not a lesson in persistence; it is a picture of how God deals with strong men, breaking the strength they trusted and giving them what they could not take.

The oath-under-the-thigh texts draw a different and lesser corruption — the embarrassed skipping of them, or the treatment of them as a curiosity of primitive custom. The gesture is doing real theological work. Abraham is sending a servant to find a wife for Isaac, and the entire promise depends on that errand; so the oath is sworn on the organ of generation, that is, on the seed itself, in the name of the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of the earth. It is the covenant promise made tangible in the most personal way available, and it belongs with circumcision, which marks the same part of the body for the same reason. Scripture is far less squeamish about the body than its readers, and the reticence is generally ours rather than the text's.
roots_summary: Hebrew yarek (thigh, loins, side) and kaph ha-yarek (the hollow or socket of the thigh); Greek meros (the thigh) in Revelation 19:16, and osphys (loins) for the related idiom.
roots_lines: Hebrew yarek (H3409) — thigh, loin, side; the word in Genesis 24:2 and 32:25, and used of the sides of the tabernacle.
Hebrew kaph (H3709) — hollow, palm, socket; joined to yarek for the hip socket dislocated at Peniel.
Hebrew gid ha-nasheh — the sinew that shrank; the tendon Israel would not eat thereafter (Genesis 32:32).
Greek meros (G3382) — the thigh; a hapax in the New Testament, occurring only at Revelation 19:16.
Greek osphys (G3751) — the loins; used in Hebrews 7:5, 10 of Levi being yet in the loins of Abraham.
usage: “Put… thy hand under my thigh” — an oath sworn on the covenant seed itself.
“The hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint” — the blessing and the crippling arrive together.
“On his thigh a name written” — the title worn where the sword hangs and every man can read it.

pos: n. (a covering for the foot; rendering Hebrew na'al, Greek hypodema, sandalion)
etymology: Old English sceoh. In Scripture the shoe is rarely just footwear: it marks holy ground when removed, transfers a legal right when handed over, and measures a man's rank by who is fit to carry or untie it.
biblical_def: The shoe in Scripture is a legal and ceremonial object. Removing it acknowledges holiness: “put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5) — the ground was not holy the day before, and Moses is barefoot because God is there. Handing it over transfers a right: “this was the manner in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning changing, for to confirm all things; a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel” (Ruth 4:7), which is how the nearer kinsman formally surrenders his claim and Boaz becomes the redeemer of Naomi's field and of Ruth. Deuteronomy gives the shaming version of the same rite, where the widow of a man who refuses to raise up his brother's name looses his shoe and spits in his face (Deuteronomy 25:9). And carrying or unloosing another man's shoes is the work of the lowest servant, which is why John the Baptist chooses it to measure the distance between himself and the One coming: “whose shoes I am not worthy to bear” (Matthew 3:11), and in Mark, not worthy to stoop down and unloose. Paul then puts shoes on the Christian: “your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6:15) — a soldier's footwear, for standing firm and for going.
webster_summary: Rarely mere footwear. Shoes come off on holy ground; a shoe handed over transfers a legal right, as when Boaz becomes redeemer; carrying another's shoes is the lowest servant's work, which John invokes; and Paul shoes the Christian with the gospel of peace.
webster_full: SHOE, n. plu. shoes. [Sax. sceo.] A covering for the foot, usually of leather, composed of a thick species for the sole, and a thinner kind for the vamp and quarters.
2. A plate of iron nailed to the hoof of a horse.
3. Among the Hebrews, the delivery of a shoe was a token of the transfer of a right or possession. Ruth 4.
4. To put off the shoes was a mark of reverence, as before holy ground. Ex. 3.
5. To bear or unloose the shoes of another was the office of the meanest slave.
scriptures: Exodus 3:5
And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
Ruth 4:7

Now this was the manner in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning changing, for to confirm all things; a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel.
Matthew 3:11
I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:
Ephesians 6:15
And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace;
corruption_summary: The Ruth shoe-ceremony is read as quaint local colour rather than as the legal machinery of redemption — and Exodus 3:5 is generalised into a sacred-places piety that Scripture's own trajectory dismantles.
corruption_paragraphs: Ruth 4 is often preached as a love story with an odd procedural interruption, but the shoe is the hinge of the book. Israel's law of redemption required a kinsman with the right, the means, and the willingness; the nearer kinsman had the first two and lacked the third, because redeeming Ruth would mar his own inheritance. He publicly surrenders his claim by handing over his shoe, and Boaz redeems field and widow together before ten elders. Every element is a type discharged in Christ — the kinsman who alone has the right, who pays the whole price, who takes a bride out of a foreign nation, and who does it at cost to himself where another would not. Luke traces the genealogy through this transaction. Treating the shoe as folklore removes the legal architecture that makes redemption a category rather than a sentiment.

Exodus 3:5 has been generalised in the other direction into a theology of sacred space: certain buildings, grounds, and objects are holy in themselves, and reverence consists in ritual behaviour toward them. The verse says the opposite of what is drawn from it. The ground is holy because God is there — it is a bush in a desert, not a shrine, and it is not recorded as venerated afterwards. Scripture's trajectory moves steadily away from holy places: the Lord Jesus tells the woman at the well that the hour comes when neither in this mountain nor at Jerusalem will men worship the Father, the veil is torn, and the temple is now the assembled people. The reverence Exodus commands is not less than the sacred-places version but more — it follows God's presence wherever it goes, which is now to a congregation of ordinary people in an ordinary room.
roots_summary: Hebrew na'al (a sandal, shoe) and chalats (to draw off, the verb of the shoe-loosing rite); Greek hypodema (that which is bound under the foot) and sandalion (a sandal).
roots_lines: Hebrew na'al (H5275) — a sandal or shoe; the word in Exodus 3:5, Ruth 4:7, and Deuteronomy 25:9.
Hebrew chalats (H2502) — to draw off, withdraw; the verb of the shoe-loosing rite, giving the name chalitzah to the ceremony.
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem as a kinsman; the legal act the shoe-transfer confirms in Ruth 4.
Greek hypodema (G5266) — a sandal, that which is bound underneath; the word in Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16.
Greek hypodeo (G5265) — to bind under, shoe; the verb in Ephesians 6:15 rendered shod.
usage: “Put off thy shoes… the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” — a bush in a desert, holy because God is there.
“A man plucked off his shoe… this was a testimony in Israel” — the legal machinery by which Boaz becomes redeemer.
“Whose shoes I am not worthy to bear” — the lowest slave's office, chosen to measure a distance.
